# Title

Mapping the Transit Gap: Neighborhood Form, Automobile Dependence, and Accessibility in the Omaha-Council Bluffs Region

# Abstract

Personal vehicle ownership can impose a substantial financial burden on households, particularly in metropolitan areas where low-density development and limited transit make driving necessary to reach employment and essential services. This study examines how neighborhood form, transit access, vehicle availability, and employment accessibility vary across Douglas and Sarpy Counties in Nebraska and Pottawattamie County in Iowa. Using the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Smart Location Database (SLD 3.0), we combine neighborhood clustering, predictive modeling, spatial accessibility analysis, and regional comparisons to investigate automobile dependence and transit equity in the Omaha-Council Bluffs metropolitan area. The clustering analysis identifies five neighborhood archetypes and reveals a clear geographic pattern: transit-accessible mixed-use centers and transit-served residential areas are concentrated in the developed urban core, while low-density peripheral areas dominate the outer portions of the region. Households without vehicles are most concentrated in the two better-served neighborhood types. Predictive modeling identifies residential density and proximity to transit stops as major drivers of household vehicle ownership. Spatial analysis also identifies transit-gap locations, including central Omaha neighborhoods and car-free block groups with limited employment accessibility. Regional comparisons further indicate that Council Bluffs generally has weaker transit and employment access than Omaha. Together, these findings provide city planners and regional agencies with a practical framework for protecting service in transit-dependent neighborhoods and prioritizing route, frequency, first- and last-mile, and land-use improvements where needs are greatest.
